lessons.title: Your goal, your constraints, your kit

blocks.markdown:
## A one-page brief

Before writing a programme, write a short **training brief**: what you want, what limits you, and what you have. It turns everything in this course into decisions.

blocks.alt: A one-page brief in four boxes: goal (one priority and a 12-week measure), constraints (days, minutes, sport days), kit (weights and space), baseline (Module 0 results).
blocks.caption: Your training brief

blocks.markdown:
## The four boxes

1. **Goal:** one priority (Module 1) and one measurable target for 12 weeks, for example 'waist −4 cm and 12 split squats with 2 × 12 kg'.
2. **Constraints:** training days and minutes, sport days, and anything to work around.
3. **Kit:** the weights and space you have (Module 3), and what you could buy next.
4. **Baseline:** your Module 0 test results, dated.

## Check it against the course

- Is the goal realistic for 12 weeks (Modules 1 and 9)?
- Do the sessions fit around sport (Modules 5 and 7)?
- Can your kit challenge you in the 6–15 rep range for the main lifts (Module 3)? If not, plan harder exercise variations or a purchase.
**What this means for your training:** write your brief on one page before touching the programme builder. Every later decision, from exercises to calories, should trace back to it.

cards.back: One page: goal and 12-week measure, constraints, kit and baseline. The source of every programme decision.
A number and a date, e.g. 'waist −4 cm and 12 split squats at 2 × 12 kg by week 12'.

options: Waist −4 cm and 20 push-ups in a row by week 12
questions.explanation: Specific and measurable, with a date.

questions.stem: Your heaviest weight lets you do 25 easy goblet squats. What does the brief flag?
options: Plan harder variations or a heavier weight
questions.explanation: Main lifts should be challenging in about 6–15 reps (Module 3).

## Three blocks of four weeks

A 12-week plan splits naturally into three **training blocks** (Module 6):

- **Weeks 1–4, learn:** technique first, 2–3 RIR, find your working weights.
- **Weeks 5–8, build:** add reps and weight with double progression; an easier week if needed.
- **Weeks 9–12, push:** same exercises or harder variations, then an easier week 12 and re-test.

blocks.alt: A 12-week timeline in three blocks: weeks 1–4 learn, weeks 5–8 build, weeks 9–11 push, week 12 easier week and re-test, with a review after each block.
blocks.caption: A 12-week plan

blocks.markdown:
## Use the programme builder

Open the programme builder from Module 5, enter your days, minutes, sport days, kit and baseline, and save the plan it gives you. Then check it against your brief: two or three full-body sessions, every main pattern covered, sessions away from match days.

blocks.title: Programme builder
blocks.description: Enter your training days, session length, sport days, kit and baseline to get a full-body A/B plan you can edit and export.

blocks.markdown:
## Add the rest of the week

Write in your daily steps target, protein range (Module 9), the warm-up and core work (Module 8) and your sport. That's the whole plan on one page.
**What this means for your training:** build the plan with the tool, then add steps, protein, warm-up, core and sport so the whole week is on one page.

cards.back: Three 4-week blocks: learn, build, push. An easier week and a re-test at week 12.
2–3 full-body sessions, all main patterns, sessions away from match days, and steps and protein written in.

lessons.title: Run it: weekly log and 4-week reviews

blocks.markdown:
## Log every session

For each exercise, write the weight, the reps in each set and the reps in reserve. Once a week, add your average weight, steps, sleep and how you felt. A notes app or paper is enough.

blocks.alt: A loop: train and log each session, a 5-minute weekly check, and a 4-week review asking what improved, what stalled and what to change, then back to training.
blocks.caption: The weekly and 4-week loop

blocks.markdown:
## The 5-minute weekly check

- Did I do the planned sessions?
- Which exercises hit the top of their rep range? Use the load helper to set next week's targets.
- Is my weekly average weight moving at the planned pace?

blocks.title: Load helper
blocks.description: Enter your rep range, weight and reps to see whether to add reps, add weight or bridge a big jump next week.

blocks.markdown:
## The 4-week review

At the end of each block, ask three questions: what improved, what stalled, and what one thing will I change? Change one thing at a time, such as an exercise variation, a set or a calorie step, so you can see what worked.
**What this means for your training:** log every session, check weekly with the load helper, and change only one thing at each 4-week review.

cards.back: Weight, reps per set and reps in reserve for each exercise; weekly average weight, steps and sleep.
What improved, what stalled, what one thing to change. One change at a time.

questions.stem: At the 4-week review, two lifts stalled and weight loss slowed. What's the best approach?
options: Change one thing, e.g. cut 150 kcal, and review again
questions.explanation: One change at a time shows what worked.

questions.stem: All sets of floor press reached 12 reps at 2 RIR. What next?
options: Use the load helper: add weight or bridge the jump
questions.explanation: Double progression: top of the range means add weight.

lessons.title: Re-test and design the next block

blocks.markdown:
## Re-test like the baseline

In week 12, repeat your Module 0 tests under the same conditions: same time of day, same warm-up, same weights. Compare push-ups, goblet squat reps, plank and side-plank holds, resting heart rate, waist and photos.

blocks.alt: Two columns, baseline and week 12, for push-ups, goblet squat reps, plank hold, resting heart rate and waist, with arrows showing direction of change and a 'next block' box.
blocks.caption: Baseline vs week 12

blocks.markdown:
## Design the next block

- **Goal met:** set the next target, or switch priority, for example from fat loss to building muscle.
- **Strength up but weights now too light:** move to harder variations or use the kit planner to choose the next purchase.
- **Stalled:** check sleep, protein, steps and logging before changing the programme.
- **Keep:** exercises you enjoy and still progress on.

## What you can now do

Pick your equipment, design a full-body programme around your sport, progress it with double progression and RIR, fit in cardio, core and mobility, eat for your goal, and judge progress with sensible measures. That's the whole course in one cycle; repeat it every 12 weeks.
**What this means for your training:** re-test in week 12 under the same conditions, write a new brief from the results, and start the next 12-week cycle.

cards.back: Same tests, same time of day, same warm-up and weights as the baseline, so the comparison is fair.
New goal or priority, harder variations or new kit, or fix sleep, protein and steps before changing the programme.

questions.stem: Why repeat the tests under the same conditions?
options: To make the results look better
So the comparison with the baseline is fair
questions.explanation: Different times or warm-ups change results.

questions.stem: Your push-ups rose from 15 to 25 and your 10 kg dumbbells now feel light for presses. What's a good next step?
options: Use harder variations or plan heavier dumbbells with the kit planner
questions.explanation: Progress the exercise or the kit.
